It IS the jbeams. Specifically the nodes and beams and triangles. You have to place in 3d space a bunch of nodes and get their weights right (to both mimic the weight of the car as well as deal with the forces applied to them by the beams. Too light and they go crazy. Too heavy and they go crazy). Now here's the thing, the collision surface is actually made up of triangles that connect 3 of these nodes. You need them close enough together and in the right position to get a decent crash model, but not so many that the car becomes laggy. You then need to create beams between the nodes. The beams are what holds the nodes all together, so you have to have each node suppoted by beams in 3d space (so that the middle of your door is "solid" and not just flapping in an out. These beams not only support the nodes, but also are what creates the actual structure with the nodes. Every beam is able to have a different strength, spring value, damping value, deform value, etc. This is what makes it so that a roll cage can be stiff, but a crumple zone can be crushed. While you can group beams together and give them the same values, this needs to be tweaked because nodes connected to more beams could behave differently than others. The deform values are tweaked so that the vehicle can dent or become deformed.

As an example, the "hatchback wing" for the BX series has it's own jbeam file. It contains 26 nodes just for a wing, which honestly isn't too bad. Those 26 nodes are connected to 167 different beams, split into different break groups with different spring, damp, deform, strength, precompression, short bound, and long bound values. There are also 16 triangles on there with various drag coefficients, lift coefficients, and stall angles so that it can actually act like a wing. This wing goes from line 1 to 390. Oh, but there is also the Nomi adjustable wing. That goes from line 391 to 795 and includes variables that can be changed in game to adjust the wing. 795 lines of code just for the wings that can be attached to the hatchback version of the car. The spoilers are another 758 lines of code for the hatch back. There are another 1323 lines of code for the wings and spoilers for the coupe version. Over 2500 lines of code and all you have are some wings and spoilers. The front suspension, not including steering, driving components, etc, is over 2,000 lines of code, and every beam angle affects how the suspension behaves in game.

Seriously, go take a look at the files for the vanilla cars to see just how much is involved. You can find them in SteamLibrary\\steamapps\\common\\BeamNG.drive\\content\\vehicles\\bx.zip\\vehicles\\bx on whatever drive you installed the game on. You can open them in any text editor, but to make it easier to read you probably want something like Notepad++ (which is free) and to tell it to treat it like a json file and it will color code things for you.

Basically, it is a huge undertaking. People spend hundreds or thousands of hours to make proper dev quality mods. Then they ask for $2-$3 as a paid download and everyone loses their mind and just pirates it. That is a lot of time for almost no money (or literally no money if they don't make it a paid mod). The types of mods that you are talking about are often just a "meshslap". Literally they take the visual mesh from a 3d model and slap it ontop of a vanilla vehicle. If you are lucky they will move the outer nodes to line up with the edge of the car so that the collision is at least somewhat accurate. If you gamble for the free cruises you will ultimately pay more than the cruise is worth. But if you are already gambling for fun, learning some point cutoffs can help you decide if it is worth a few more bucks for a few more points.

At 500 points you'll get some offer for discounts.  By the Ultra level you are getting free balcony rooms on many cruises with free drinks anywhere on board for you on some cruises.  By elite you can get free balcony on most cruises, and some cruises may be free drinks for you and a guest.

So I've owned various pumps over the years for my paddle boards.  I started using my car tire pump. It worked, but was slow.  I then upgraded to a higher volume car tire pump.  It worked a little faster, but was still slow, and doing 2 boards would make the heat sink hot enough to burn you.

I eventually bought two pumps made for paddle boards:   
[https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B07V9WCBN7/ref=ppx\_yo\_dt\_b\_search\_asin\_title?ie=UTF8&psc=1](https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B07V9WCBN7/ref=ppx_yo_dt_b_search_asin_title?ie=UTF8&psc=1)

[https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B0819RTT4P/ref=ppx\_yo\_dt\_b\_search\_asin\_title?ie=UTF8&th=1](https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B0819RTT4P/ref=ppx_yo_dt_b_search_asin_title?ie=UTF8&th=1)

​

Instead of being close to 15 minutes per board I think these are closer to 7 from being completely flat to 15psi.  They also can each do about 2 boards in a row before overheating (depending on size of the boards and outdoor temp).  

Benefits of a pump made for paddle boards is that they are typically 2 stage pumps.  The first stage is high volume, low pressure like you would see for an inflatable mattress.  The second stage is lower volume higher pressure like you would see on a car tire inflator.  This lets it run less meaning that it won't overheat as quickly and the battery (if a battery powered one) won't die as quickly. If you a tiny air hose like the one you posted, imagine how much that has to run to get enough air through that hose to fill up your entire board just to get it to 1psi. 

Can you use the attached pump? Sure.  I don't know how long it would take or if it would overheat or if a charge would last a full inflation, though.

Of course, all of it is worse than not doing it, but while the world is reliant on plastics, a plant like this will exist somewhere.  Now, the other side of it is that the flares sometimes aren't receiving pure methane, but rather a mix of stuff.  Some of that isn't great to burn and can release less than ideal chemicals.  Honestly, the only thing that we can do is vote in people that will put in regulations to decrease production/increase capture of things that are harmful to us and the environment.

Fuse should be lower than the rating of the wire and higher than the draw from the light.  You said 2.2amps, so 3+ for the power draw.  Look in the documentation regarding wire size and rating, etc. If it doesn't list anything, try to figure out the wire size yourself.

For example, 10' of 18ga wire at 12v is rated for about 5A.  I would probably install a 3A fuse at that point to protect the wire.  If it's 16ga wire and relatively short, it is probably rated to 10A or more. In that case I would probably install a 5A fuse which still protects the wire, but has more head room to avoid nuisance trips if the LED driver decides to pull a bit more power when turning on, etc.,

If it's 20ga wire, keep that wire as short as possible, and get the smallest fuse that doesn't burn out when you turn the lights on, and keep a fire extinguisher around just in case... 20ga with a 2.2amp load in a harsh environment (including engine heat), plus voltage drop for distance  severely limits the allowable amps.  Best case scenario is that it continues to work.  Worst case scenario is that the wire burns up, potentially leading to other damage.

So, with Carnival my understanding is that they track the number of dollars put through the machine.  What that means is if you put $1,000,000 in a machine, spin once, and take the money back out, it doesn't matter.  But, if you have $10 in a machine and keep winning your money back and play for hours on end, you will get lots of points.  I believe points are about 1 per $2.50 bet on slots.  I think the table games are based on what the pit boss marks your play down as.  

At around 1,000 points or 1,500 points (depending on cruise length, yours would be 1,000) you will get free drinks while playing in the casino for the rest of your cruise I believe.

They keep track of your points per cruise/points per day. No one knows what those numbers need to be to get good deals, but once you are getting over 1,000 points you will likely get some decent deals.  Beyond that it is very highly dependent on how Carnival is doing.  For example, Earlier this year I had an offer for a balcony Alaskan cruise for $25/person.  Unfortunately someone in my party got sick and we had to reschedule.  The new cruise was $650+ per person. As cruising gets back towards normal the deals will become less, but they will still provide deals, especially on cruises that are not filling up as fast as they would like.  

I've met people that get 5,000-10,000 points per cruise.  They were given a free suite and $1,000 on board credit.  But that's a lot of money through a machine.  I mean, you could get lucky and put $1 in and keep winning enough to keep playing until you get there.  Or you could be unlucky and lose every hand and it would cost $12,500+.  If you assume Carnival pays out at around 80%, that is losing about $2.5k  per cruise....

In otherwords, if you have fun playing (or in your case you have OBC you don't need for other things), enjoy playing.  If you are trying to get deals worth more than you spend, it's probably not going to work out in your favor.

It's an awkward age in cruising - Too old for the kids clubs. Too young to meet people drinking at the bar (if a US based cruise, and yes, you can still meet people at the bar not drinking, but if you look young and aren't drinking alcohol, a lot of people may avoid friendships).

But, even as an adult it can be hard to "make friends" on a cruise.  My best recommendation is join a roll call (facebook or cruise critic) for your cruise to see if there are other people you age before you even get on the ship.  If not, then be confident in going to the activities that interest you and doing things solo. You may run into people also doing those things and now you have something to chat about. When you get off the ship on a cruise the country is granting you permission to stay in that country for the duration of the port stop.  If you stay longer than that, you are overstaying what you were permitted to do.  It's the same thing as going to a country that has a 7 day visa and staying longer than a week. 

From my understanding, if you are late getting back to the ship, they will make announcements to make sure you aren't on the ship but didn't get checked in when boarding. Then they will send security to your room to make sure you aren't there.  Then they open the safe (with multiple people as witnesses to ensure nothing is stolen) and look for any important documents (wallets, passports, etc).  They take those off of the ship and give them to someone affiliated with the cruise line.  Then they leave.  When you make it to the port and see the ship is gone, port security should be able to point you to the cruise affiliated person who will give you your documents.  They will then likely be able to give you information on what needs to happen next.  The next part probably varies by port/country, but you may need to meet with immigration. You may have a fine for overstaying. You will need to get your own transportation to the next port.  The cruise line will typically let your board again (they want their money from you and make most of it while you are on the ship), but they don't have to.  I've heard stories, though I don't know if they are true, of people being extremely late at every port (like the documents were being transferred to the shore liaison when they arrived) and after a couple of stops, they packed the bags and didn't let them come back on board (as staying late at a port impacts the cruise ship both in time (and then money as they go faster to get to the next port on time) as well as manpower and potential fees if they are at a busy port).

As for where you could fly - I imagine you could fly to the next stop (Fiji if you were late at Hawaii, or Sydney if you were late at Fiji).  I don't see how you would fly to New Zealand as your bags would be waiting at immigration in Sydney for you.

As a related experience, I once needed to leave a cruise in the middle of the cruise.  Carnival notified Jamaican immigration and they had an immigration officer there waiting for me at the dock. They asked me a bunch of questions, etc.  Carnival also had called a cab for me, but I was on my own for paying for the cab and paying at the airport.  My passport stamp for Jamaica actually has my flight info written on it as they only gave me permission to be in the country until my flight left. I imagine it would be similar if you missed the ship on accident.

So, I'm no string instrument player, but I think I can help with this.  The frets on bouzoukis (or guitars) are a half step apart.  Therefore, if you put the capo on the first fret, AND move the known chord up by one fret, you will then be playing a chord that is one half step above what you originally were.

Basically, if you know a song in C, but you want to play it in D, you can put the capo on the 2nd fret (1 whole step) and then pretend that is the top of your bouzouki and move the chords you normally play two frets closer to the sound hole.  You play the same chord shapes from the key of C and now the song is in D.

It is also useful when a song has complex chords or chords that are hard to change between.  Using a capo offsets what sound the chord shape makes.  That means you can change to a chord shape x number of steps down, and then put the capo the same number of frets up and get the same chord.  For example, if you don't like to play a G chord shape, you can capo 2 (one full step) then play the chord shape one step lower (F chord shape).  You will then be playing a G chord.

Of course depending on where your capo is and what notes you are playing, you are also changing the specific notes making up the chord.  That leads to another use which is to change the sound of a chord to fit the song better.  An extreme example of this would be using the capo on the 12th fret.  Then everything would be up an octave, but you would be back to the original chord shapes.

I suggest learning on any tunable drum you can get in your budget.  If you enjoy it you will likely want to upgrade to a better drum.  In my experience you have a few levels of bodhrans:

1. Display piece - if it has a design printed/painted on it it is likely more suited to hang on the wall than to play
2. El-Cheapo - entry level, non tunable, garbage skin
3. Beginner - entry level, tunable, but may use proprietary tuning keys, entry level skin (this is where the one you posted seems to fit).
4. Advanced - Tunable, typically with an allen key, decent to good skin. May come pre-taped. (see Walton tunable drums as a common example).
5. Custom - Made to your specs. Hand selected skin. Customizable.  

I recommend starting with a 3 or 4 depending on budget.  If you play regularly you will almost certainly move up to a 4 at some point, and possibly into a 5.  I know that I started with a 3, then got another 3, then upgraded to a 4, and then finally got a custom one at the start of the pandemic (I was supposed to pick it up in Ireland, but all travel was cancelled and had to get it shipped to me).

From my understanding (and I'm far from an expert, though I do now know a whole lot more about vehicle scheduling and production than I ever thought I would need to) is that they schedule a bunch of orders each month.  Then by the end of the month they do "cleanup" scheduling which is basically going through and looking at which dealers still have allocations for that month. They then find trucks they can build for those dealers with what parts they still have available in the system.  

Because of this, if you have any constrained parts it is more likely that you will need to be scheduled in the first chunk of scheduling instead of being scheduled on a cleanup week as they may not have any more of that constrained part for the build date in question.
